# Create .ruff.toml to align lint rules with project conventions

## Problem Statement

Running `ruff check . --select ALL` produces ~17,000 errors, the vast majority of which are from rules (ANN* for missing annotations, S101 for `assert`, T201 for `print()`) that do not align with project conventions. The project lacks a ruff configuration file, so there is no way to filter rules, set conventions (line length, target Python), or exclude test-specific patterns.

## Users

- **Developers** — Currently see ~17K lint errors, making it impossible to use ruff meaningfully for catching real issues.
- **Code reviewers** — Without config, lint-guided review is impractical.

**User stories:**
- As a developer, I want `ruff check .` to produce < 100 actionable warnings so I can use it as part of my development workflow.
- As a code reviewer, I want the project's lint conventions documented in a config file so I can enforce them consistently.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `.ruff.toml` file created at repo root with project-specific configuration.
- [ ] Rule set selected that matches documented project conventions (see Key Files for baseline recommendation).
- [ ] `ruff check .` produces < 100 consistent, actionable warnings.
- [ ] Per-file ignores configured for test directories (`tests/`, `proxy/tests/`) to permit `assert` (S101) and `print` (T201) if those rules are enabled (future-proofing; not required for the baseline rule set).
- [ ] Config is documented in README or contributing guide.
- [ ] All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
- [ ] Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.
- [ ] Baseline `ruff check --fix` run included to resolve auto-fixable violations so the < 100 threshold is met.

> **Note:** CHANGELOG.md is excluded from this list — it is managed automatically by the release pipeline. Implementing agents must not manually update CHANGELOG.md.

## Constraints

- `ruff` version currently available: **0.15.21** (in `.venv/bin/ruff`)
- Must not modify existing `.gitignore` or agent framework files
- Config file must be a standalone `.ruff.toml` (no `pyproject.toml` exists in the repo)
- Must not introduce rules that would require large-scale refactoring beyond auto-fix

## Existing State

- No `.ruff.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `.flake8`, or `setup.cfg` with lint config at repo root.
- ruff is installed in `.venv` at version 0.15.21.
- `ruff check . --select ALL` produces **16,823 errors** covering 90+ rule categories.
- The project uses Python 3.12.3; `.venv/bin/python3` is 3.12.

## Desired Change

1. Create `.ruff.toml` at repo root with:
   - `target-version = "py312"` (environment runs 3.12)
   - `line-length = 120` (project code consistently uses long lines)
   - Rule `select`: `["F", "E", "W", "I", "N", "UP", "RUF100"]`
   - Rule `ignore`: `["E501"]` (line-length is advisory)
   - Per-file-ignores for test directories
2. Run `ruff check --fix` to resolve auto-fixable violations (~968 errors, all auto-fixable)
3. Run `ruff check .` to verify < 100 remaining warnings (expected: 0 after fix)
4. Update README or contributing guide with lint usage instructions

## Key Files (predicted)

- `.ruff.toml` — **New file.** Main ruff configuration file at repo root.
- `README.md` — Add section on running lint checks with ruff.
- `tests/` and `proxy/tests/` — Per-file-ignores in `.ruff.toml` for test-specific patterns.

## Related Work

- **LP-0MROX8F610024YL9** — "Run ruff check --fix to resolve 223 auto-fixable lint errors" (completed). Prior lint cleanup that resolved F401, F541, F811 errors.
- **LP-0MROYEVL3004Y04Z** — "Manually fix remaining 5 non-auto-fixable lint errors (4 F401, 1 F811)" (open). Manual fixup for non-auto-fixable errors excluded from the above.
- **LP-0MROX8F69003JPAB** — "Fix 27 ambiguous variable names (E741) for readability" (completed). Explicitly excluded E741 from the auto-fix pass.
- **LP-0MROX8F6600331RO** — "Fix 51 unused variable warnings (F841) across codebase" (completed). Another prior lint cleanup.



## Related work (automated report)

The automated find_related search was run but returned no new related work items beyond those listed in the manual Related Work section above. Repository keyword matches were broad (mostly infrastructure files, worktree copies from unrelated work items) and did not identify any additional actionable related work.

---

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

- Q: "Which config file format to use — `.ruff.toml` or `pyproject.toml`?"
  - **Answer:** `.ruff.toml` — no `pyproject.toml` exists in the repo, and creating one solely for ruff adds unnecessary complexity. Source: repo inspection.

- Q: "What target Python version?"
  - **Answer:** `py312` — the environment runs Python 3.12.3. Source: `.venv/bin/python3 --version`.

- Q: "Should additional auto-fixable rules like COM812 (trailing commas) or Q000 (quote style) be included?"
  - **Answer:** Not for this work item — the baseline set (F, E, W, I, N, UP, RUF100) after `--fix` gives 0 errors, satisfying the < 100 AC. Additional rules can be added in a follow-up. Source: analysis of `ruff check . --select F,E,W,I,N,UP,RUF100 --ignore E501`.

- Q: "What line-length setting?"
  - **Answer:** `120` — consistently used in existing code; 1,494 E501 violations confirm the project doesn't follow 88-char PEP 8. Source: repo inspection and ruff statistics.

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Scope-creep risk:** The baseline config (F, E, W, I, N, UP, RUF100) yields 0 non-fixable errors after `--fix`, which satisfies the AC. There is a risk of expanding scope to include more rules (COM812, Q000, SIM prefixed rules). These should be tracked as separate work items rather than added here.
- **Auto-fix risk:** `ruff check --fix` modifies source files. All changes are auto-fixable, but developers should review the diff before committing. The fix run should be done as a separate commit from the `.ruff.toml` addition for audit clarity.
- **Test-suite risk:** Auto-fix changes (particularly UP045/UP006 PEP 604 annotations and I001 import reordering) could alter semantics. Run the full test suite after `—fix` and commit only if all tests pass.
- **Compatibility:** ruff 0.15.21 is currently installed. If ruff is upgraded to a newer version, the config may need minor updates. Document the required ruff version in README.
- **Assumption:** The team agrees with the recommended rule set (F, E, W, I, N, UP, RUF100). If preferred rules differ, the AC "Rules selected match project conventions" allows adjustment.
data.title: Create .ruff.toml to align lint rules with project conventions

data.title: Manually fix remaining 5 non-auto-fixable lint errors (4 F401, 1 F811)

data.description:
## Problem

The proxy's smart-routing system maintains its own `_model_cache_cold` / `_session_cache_cold` state machine to decide whether to bypass local Qwen3 for large-context requests. This inferred state is unreliable because:

1. **Streaming success path** (provider.py:1939) defers session-based cache warming to router.py via the `not _session_id` guard
2. **Router slot-save callback** (router.py:426) never fires with scheduler-based slot management because `slot_enabled=False`
3. The non-streaming path (provider.py:2265) works correctly, but pi always uses streaming
4. Result: session caches are **never marked warm**, so once the accumulated conversation exceeds `local_large_context_cold_cache_threshold` (30K tokens), ALL subsequent requests bypass local Qwen3

## Users

- **Proxy operator (Map):** runs LLM workloads through the proxy. Current incorrect cache-cold behavior causes all large-context sessions to bypass local Qwen3 after crossing 30K tokens, wasting remote API calls and increasing latency. Fixing this restores correct local routing for sessions with warm caches.
- **Agents running through pi:** experience degraded performance as their long-running sessions are incorrectly routed to remote providers, adding latency and cost.

### User Stories

- As an operator, I want warm-cache sessions to route to local Qwen3 even when the conversation exceeds 30K tokens, so that I avoid unnecessary remote API round-trips and keep inference fast.
- As an operator, I want sessions with truly cold caches (e.g., after slot reassignment or a reasoning stall) to correctly bypass local for large contexts, so that the proxy doesn't block on GPU prefill.
- As a maintainer, I want the routing decision to be based on actual KV cache state (cached_tokens from llama.cpp) rather than inferred state flags, so that the system is robust and understandable.

## Solution

Replace the entire inferred cache-cold state machine with a simple reactive approach that uses the **actual `cached_tokens` value** from llama.cpp's response.

### How it works

After each local response, extract `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` from the usage data (already present in llama.cpp's SSE response). Store the ratio of cached/prompt tokens per (model, session_id).

Before routing a request to local, check:

    if last_cached_ratio < 1 AND estimated_tokens > cold_threshold:
        skip local (cache wasn't fully warm on last request)

A ratio of 1.0 means ALL tokens were cached (fully warm). Anything less means at least some tokens needed recomputation.

### Legacy code to remove (no backward compatibility required)

All of the following must be deleted entirely:

- `_model_cache_cold`, `_session_cache_cold`, `_model_cache_cold_uninitialized` globals in proxy/provider.py
- `is_model_cache_cold()`, `clear_model_cache_cold()`, `mark_model_cache_cold()` functions
- `initialize_cache_cold_from_config()`, `_cache_cold_initialized()` functions
- `on_slot_save_success()` and all call sites
- `_release_session_slot_for_cache_cold_bypass()` and its call site
- The `not _session_id` guard from the streaming success path
- The `cache_cold_large_context` fallback reason and all references
- `_get_large_context_cold_cache_threshold()` and `_get_large_context_warm_cache_threshold()`
- `local_large_context_cold_cache_threshold`, `local_large_context_warm_cache_threshold` config keys
- `_should_skip_local()` and `_estimate_prompt_tokens_for_routing()` rewired to use cached_tokens ratio instead of cache-cold flag
- Model `token_estimate_multiplier` config key if it's only used with the old cache-cold logic
- Any references to above in tests

### What gets added

- A simple in-memory dict `_last_cached_ratio: dict[tuple[str, str], float]`
- Extraction of `cached_tokens` from the SSE usage event in router_helpers.py
- A simplified routing check that compares stored ratio against the cold threshold

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All listed legacy code removed (no backward compatibility stubs or deprecation wrappers)
- [ ] All existing smart-routing tests pass with the new approach
- [ ] Session 019f707c no longer incorrectly bypasses local Qwen3 after the cold-cache threshold is crossed
- [ ] Session 019f7076 correctly bypasses local Qwen3 after the reasoning stall (cached_tokens will be 0)
- [ ] No regression in warm-cache sessions (cached_tokens ratio >= 1)
- [ ] `cached_tokens` extraction added to the usage parser in router_helpers.py
- [ ] No dead code or imports left behind from the removed system
- [ ] All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
- [ ] Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

> **Note:** CHANGELOG.md is excluded from this list — it is managed automatically by the ship skill's release pipeline.

## Constraints

- **No backward compatibility stubs:** All cache-cold functions must be deleted entirely, not deprecated with wrappers.
- **Streaming path only:** pi always uses streaming; non-streaming behavior is irrelevant for this fix.
- **Tokenizer mismatch:** The estimated prompt tokens use OpenAI's cl100k_base tokenizer, which differs from Qwen3's native tokenizer by ~13–15%. The existing `token_estimate_multiplier` config compensates for this — if it's only used in the old cache-cold logic, decide whether to keep or remove it.
- **Slot scheduler integration:** The `on_slot_save_success` callback never fires because `slot_enabled=False` with the scheduler — any replacement approach must not depend on this callback.

## Existing State

- All cache-cold state machine code lives in `proxy/provider.py` (~120 lines of globals + functions)
- Cache-cold functions are called from `proxy/server.py` (startup initialization), `proxy/session.py` (on invalidation), and `proxy/lifecycle.py` (on model switch)
- Smart routing in `proxy/provider.py` (`proxy_with_fallback`) uses `_should_skip_local()` and `_estimate_effective_prompt_tokens_for_routing()` with the cache-cold flag
- No `cached_tokens` extraction exists anywhere in the codebase yet
- Test files: `proxy/tests/test_smart_routing.py`, `proxy/tests/test_provider_fallback.py`, `proxy/tests/test_lifespan_phases_parity.py`

## Desired Change

1. **Remove** all cache-cold state machine code from `proxy/provider.py`
2. **Add** `_last_cached_ratio` dict and extraction of `cached_tokens` from llama.cpp SSE usage responses in `router_helpers.py`
3. **Rewire** routing logic to use `cached_tokens` ratio instead of cache-cold flag
4. **Remove** `cache_cold_large_context` fallback reason and related config keys
5. **Remove** or simplify `_should_skip_local()` and `_estimate_prompt_tokens_for_routing()`
6. **Update** call sites in `proxy/server.py`, `proxy/session.py`, `proxy/lifecycle.py`
7. **Update** tests to match new routing logic

## Key Files (predicted)

- `proxy/proxy/provider.py` — Remove ~120 lines of cache-cold globals and functions; rewire routing logic in `proxy_with_fallback`
- `proxy/proxy/router_helpers.py` — Add `cached_tokens` extraction from SSE usage events
- `proxy/proxy/server.py` — Remove `_startup_initialize_cache_cold_start()` call and `initialize_cache_cold_from_config` import
- `proxy/proxy/session.py` — Remove `mark_model_cache_cold` call on invalidation
- `proxy/proxy/lifecycle.py` — Remove `clear_model_cache_cold` call on model switch
- `proxy/tests/test_smart_routing.py` — Rewrite tests to use cached_tokens ratio instead of cache-cold flag
- `proxy/tests/test_provider_fallback.py` — Update fallback tests affected by the change
- `proxy/tests/test_lifespan_phases_parity.py` — Remove or update cache-cold initialization tests

## Related Work

- **LP-0MRDE669Y003V1SO** — "Fix cache-cold bypass: large-context routing never triggers for first request and after restart" (completed): Previous fix for the same underlying issue using the old state machine approach — addresses the flag lifecycle but retains the unreliable inferred-state pattern.
- **LP-0MRMMBZ7T007ER59** — "Per-session cache warm/cold tracking instead of model-level flag" (completed): Replaced model-level `_model_cache_cold: set[str]` with session-level `_session_cache_cold: dict`. Still relies on inferred state — predecessor to this work.
- **LP-0MRE4NBQ5009V5BX** — "Add dual-threshold large-context routing bypass (cold-cache + warm-cache)" (completed): Added warm-cache threshold in addition to cold-cache threshold. Extended the state machine without fixing its fundamental unreliability.
- **LP-0MRGUJ3QR002K18G** — "Release local model slot immediately when session is routed to remote fallback" (completed): Added `_release_session_slot_for_cache_cold_bypass()` — this function and its call site will be removed.
- **LP-0MRCSSBTM002NK3B** — "Investigate and fix local Qwen3 request timeout" (completed): Original cache-cold bypass implementation that introduced the `not _session_id` guard now being removed.

## Risks & Assumptions

- **cached_tokens availability:** Assumes llama.cpp's SSE response always includes `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. If a particular llama-server version omits this field, the new routing will default to assuming a cold cache (conservative). Mitigation: default `last_cached_ratio` to 0.0 (cold) when no usage data is available.
- **Token count mismatch with cached tokens:** The `cached_tokens` field reports tokens cached by the KV cache, not the prompt token count. The ratio calculation `cached / total_prompt_tokens` handles this correctly.
- **Scope creep — config cleanup:** The `token_estimate_multiplier` and threshold config keys may be used elsewhere or by external operators. Verify before removal.
- **Scope creep — test coverage expansion:** The existing test suite covers both cold and warm cache paths. Adding tests for `cached_tokens` parsing is in scope; a full test overhaul is not.
- **First-request race condition:** On the first request to a new session (or after a model switch), `_last_cached_ratio` has no entry. The routing logic must default to conservative (assume ratio=0.0 = cold) to avoid routing large contexts to a cold cache.
- **Unbounded memory growth:** `_last_cached_ratio` is a per-(model, session_id) dict with no eviction policy. Over extended operation this could grow without bound. Mitigation: cap at a reasonable configurable limit (e.g., 1000 entries) with LRU eviction, or piggyback on session cleanup.

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

### Round 1

- **Q:** "The existing description is very detailed. Are there any additional constraints, environment details, or edge cases I should capture?" — Answer (user): "Proceed with the information provided — it's comprehensive enough to draft the intake brief."

### Open Questions (to be confirmed during implementation)

- **Config key independence:** Are `local_large_context_cold_cache_threshold` and `local_large_context_warm_cache_threshold` used ONLY in the cache-cold routing logic? If shared with other features (e.g., metrics, UI display), they may need to remain as config settings even after the routing logic changes.
- **token_estimate_multiplier ownership:** Is this config key specific to the old cache-cold routing? If it's used by the new cached_tokens ratio logic (to correct tokenizer mismatch before comparing against the threshold), it should be preserved.

## Problem statement

Add a new friendly model alias `author` with the same cascade fallback chain as the existing `plan` model, so callers can use an `author` role-specific model that resolves via the same provider stack (local Qwen3 → remote OpenCode free → OpenCode Go → DeepSeek).

## Users

- Pi agent skills and AI workflows that require an authoring/editing model (e.g., draft generation, content revision, documentation authoring) distinct from `plan` (strategy/reasoning) or `code` (implementation).
- Backend services and scripts wanting a stable, human-friendly model name for authoring tasks without knowing internal model IDs.
- Operators and infra teams wanting the `author` alias to be configurable in `proxy/config.yaml` — no code changes needed to add or remap it.

### Example User Stories

- As an agent skill developer, I want to use `"model": "author"` in API requests so that content drafting and revision tasks route to the Qwen3 model with appropriate fallback, without requiring callers to know internal model IDs.
- As an operator, I want `author` to have an identical fallback chain to `plan` so that both role-based aliases have consistent reliability and failover behaviour.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The proxy accepts `model: "author"` (exact match, case-insensitive) and routes requests to the configured preset with the same fallback chain as `plan`.
2. The `author` model entry in `proxy/config.yaml` has an identical providers list to `plan`: local Qwen3 → OpenCode free → OpenCode Go → DeepSeek.
3. The `author` alias has `force_full_prompt: true` (matching `plan`).
4. `/v1/models` lists `author` as a standalone model entry with alias `["author"]`.
5. New unit/integration tests verify `author` alias resolution, routing, and `/v1/models` listing — following the same pattern as the existing `test_alias_plan_code_integration.py`.

7. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.

> **Note:** CHANGELOG.md is **excluded** from this list. It is managed automatically by the ship skill's release pipeline.

## Constraints

- Must be config-driven only (`proxy/config.yaml` entry) — no code changes to routing logic, alias resolution, or the `/v1/models` handler.
- Must not change existing alias behaviour, routing logic, or break existing `plan`/`code`/`embeddings` mappings (backwards compatible).
- Must follow the exact alias semantics used by `plan` and `code` (exact match via existing fnmatch/wildcard infrastructure).

## Existing state

- The `plan` model has a 4-tier cascade fallback chain: local `qwen3` → `opencode-deepseek-free` → `opencode-go-deepseek` → `deepseek-v4-flash`.
- `proxy/tests/test_alias_plan_code_integration.py` provides the test pattern for alias resolution, routing, and `/v1/models` listing.

## Desired change

- Add tests to `proxy/tests/test_alias_author_integration.py` (or extend the existing alias test file) covering:

## Key Files

- `proxy/config.yaml` — Add `author` model entry with identical providers list to `plan`.
- `proxy/tests/test_alias_plan_code_integration.py` — Add `author` tests (or create a new `test_alias_author_integration.py` following the same pattern).
- `proxy/README.md` — Update the friendly model aliases table/section to include `author`.

## Related work

- **Support friendly model aliases: embeddings, plan, code** (LP-0MNTB69NS0031ZO2) — Parent epic that established the friendly alias pattern. Completed; the `plan` and `code` config entries, tests, and documentation set the precedent for `author`.
- **Alias routing tests** (LP-0MQ5BMQTH0019IOY) — Child of the epic above; established integration test patterns for alias resolution, routing, and `/v1/models` listing. These tests serve as the template for `author` tests.
- **Documentation: friendly aliases** (LP-0MQ5BN49N005NFSR) — Updated `proxy/README.md` and `proxy/MODEL_ADD.md` with plan/code alias guidance; author will follow the same doc pattern.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: "Alias pattern: plan uses plan* (wildcard) while code uses exact match code. Should author be an exact match alias (author) or wildcard (author*)?" — Answer (user): "exact". Source: interactive reply.
- Q: "Local model: Should the local backend use the same qwen3 (like plan), or a different local model?" — Answer (user): "same". Source: interactive reply. Implies `llama_model: Qwen3`.

## Summary

Extend the existing backend self-healing watchdog and the `/health` endpoint to cover the TTS (qwentts) server — detect when it crashes, report its status via `/health`, and automatically restart it.

## Problem statement

The proxy's self-healing infrastructure (`backend_health.py` → `_backend_watchdog_loop`) currently only monitors and revives the llama-server. If the TTS server (`tts-server`) crashes or becomes unresponsive, there is no automated detection or recovery — it requires manual intervention. Additionally, the `/health` endpoint provides no visibility into TTS server status.

## Users

- **Primary**: On-call operators who rely on automatic recovery and the `/health` endpoint for system state.
- **Secondary**: Developers debugging TTS-related issues who need to know whether the TTS server is healthy.

### User Stories

- As an operator, I want the proxy's `/health` endpoint to report TTS server status so I can monitor it without manual checks.
- As an operator, I want the system to automatically restart a crashed TTS server so TTS functionality recovers without manual intervention.
- As a developer, I want TTS self-healing events to be logged with the same detail as llama-server recovery events for triage.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The `/health` endpoint includes a `tts_server_running` field (boolean), reflecting whether the `tts_process` is alive (`poll() is None`).
2. The `/health` endpoint includes a `tts_server_healthy` field (boolean), determined by probing `http://localhost:<tts_port>/health` (which returns `{"status": "ok"}`).
3. A new background watchdog loop (or extension of the existing loop) monitors the TTS server process and attempts automatic restart when it exits or becomes unhealthy.
4. TTS server restarts follow a similar but simpler pattern to llama-server self-healing: configurable max attempts and backoff, with clear logging.
5. TTS self-healing respects the `tts_enabled` config flag — no monitoring or restarts when disabled.
6. Tests verify: (a) `/health` reports TTS status accurately (alive, dead, disabled), (b) watchdog restarts a dead TTS process within the configured limits, (c) TTS watchdog respects `tts_enabled=false`.
7. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
8. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- Must not interfere with existing llama-server watchdog or model health loops.
- TTS self-healing should be independent (parallel loop) to avoid coupling recovery behaviors.
- Must respect the existing `tts_enabled` configuration flag.
- Must not introduce new dependencies beyond those already in use (httpx, asyncio, subprocess).

## Existing state

- The proxy tracks `tts_process` (a `subprocess.Popen | None` global in `server.py`).
- `lifecycle.py` has `start_tts_server()`, `stop_tts_server()`, and `wait_for_tts_server()` for startup/shutdown.
- The `/health` endpoint (`handlers.py` → `health_check()`) reports llama-server state but has **no** TTS fields.
- The self-healing watchdog (`backend_health.py` → `_backend_watchdog_loop`) only monitors llama-server.
- The TTS server exposes a `/health` endpoint returning `{"status": "ok"}` when healthy.
- TTS config: `tts_enabled`, `tts_server_port` (default 8081), `tts_server_host`, `tts_start_script`.

## Desired change

1. **`/health` endpoint**: Add `tts_server_running` (process alive) and `tts_server_healthy` (HTTP probe) fields.
2. **TTS watchdog task**: Add a new `_tts_watchdog_loop()` in `backend_health.py` (or a new module) that periodically checks the TTS process and restarts it if dead. Follow the existing backoff/max-attempts pattern but simpler (lower defaults).
3. **Lifecycle integration**: Wire the TTS watchdog into `server.py` lifespan (start/stop alongside existing watchdog tasks).
4. **Config**: Add TTS self-heal config keys (`tts_self_heal_max_attempts`, `tts_self_heal_window_seconds`, etc.) with sensible defaults.
5. **Tests**: Extend or create test cases for the new TTS watchdog and health fields.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` — Add TTS watchdog loop (`_tts_watchdog_loop`) and helpers.
- `proxy/proxy/handlers.py` — Extend `health_check()` to include TTS status fields.
- `proxy/proxy/server.py` — Wire TTS watchdog launch/shutdown into lifespan.
- `proxy/config.yaml` — Add TTS self-heal configuration defaults.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_integration.py` — Extend with TTS health endpoint tests.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_watchdog.py` — New file for TTS watchdog self-healing tests.

## Related work

- **TTS Server Lifecycle Management (LP-0MQVJ76WP009QOUE)** — Completed. Established TTS startup/shutdown and initial health check during startup. This work extends that foundation with ongoing monitoring and automatic recovery.
- **Detect and self-heal llama-server GPU crash states via health endpoint (LP-0MQ0ZHA4H006TUNE)** — Completed. Established the watchdog and self-healing pattern (backoff, max attempts, `/health` fields) that this work will mirror for TTS.
- **Extract Observability Module (LP-0MPU11WP3002RLEF)** — Completed. Established observability patterns used by `/health`.

## Risks & Assumptions

- Risk: TTS watchdog false positives if network hiccup briefly; mitigation: use a consecutive-failure threshold (similar to model health loop), not single-failure trigger.
- Risk: Restart loop if TTS binary is broken; mitigation: cap max attempts within a window, log clearly, escalate to operator.
- Risk: Scope creep into TTS server improvements; mitigation: limit to monitoring + restart — no changes to TTS binary itself.
- Assumption: TTS server health is probed via its `/health` endpoint with a short timeout (2s).
- Assumption: TTS server does not need the same zombie-process detection as llama-server — simple process-exit detection is sufficient.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: "Should the TTS watchdog use the same fuzzy warm as the existing llama-server watchdog? Or run as a separate loop?" — Answer (inferred from code structure + user intent): Separate loop is safer to avoid coupling recovery behaviors between two independent services. Source: code review — llama-server watchdog handles router-mode complexity (zombie detection, port probing) that is irrelevant to TTS.
- Q: "Does the TTS server have its own health endpoint?" — Answer (discovered via research): Yes, `http://localhost:8081/health` returns `{"status": "ok"}`. Source: active probing.
- Q: "Should the /health endpoint reflect TTS status even when tts_enabled=false?" — Answer (inferred): Yes, report `tts_server_running: false` and `tts_server_healthy: false` with `tts_enabled: false` so operators can distinguish disabled from crashed. Source: existing design pattern with backend_recovery state.
data.title: Extend self-healing to monitor and revive TTS server and include TTS status in /health endpoint

## Summary

Remove the JobScheduler admission queuing layer (slot_management) entirely. The dispatch lease system (session_slot_pool_size) already handles concurrency gating, session ownership, and timeout-based release. The JobScheduler adds ~430 lines of code, a config section, and a slot-leak bug all for marginal benefit.

## Why Remove

Analysis of Qwen3 slot activity logs and code review revealed:

1. **Redundant concurrency gating**: The dispatch lease system (_try_acquire_local_dispatch in router_helpers.py) already limits concurrent local requests to session_slot_pool_size (2). Same-session re-acquisition is always permitted. Inactive leases expire after 60s. This covers everything the JobScheduler was meant to provide.

2. **Slot leak bug**: When _try_acquire_local_dispatch() denies a request (router.py line 723), the code returns 503 with no cleanup mark_request_end() or remove_job() are never called. The scheduler slot stays in Owned state with active_requests=1, only recovered after max_request_duration (600s) via the background timeout check.

3. **Architectural confusion**: Two separate slot systems (JobScheduler pool_size=4, dispatch leases max=2) with different config keys, different behaviors, and unclear interactions.

4. **Multi-backend irrelevance**: The JobScheduler doesn't participate in backend routing. Future multi-llama-server support requires per-backend dispatch leases and provider-level fallback which is orthogonal to the JobScheduler.

## Files to Change

### Remove entirely
- proxy/proxy/slot_scheduler.py (the full JobScheduler class, ~430 lines)

### Remove imports and code in
- proxy/proxy/router.py: Import, globals, _get_job_scheduler(), _scheduler_has_idle_slot(), _scheduler_session_has_slot(), admission logic (lines ~570-608), _release_scheduler_and_decrement(), slot_lock_coordinator.set_scheduler()
- proxy/proxy/provider.py: _get_scheduler_has_idle_slot(), _get_scheduler_session_has_slot(), slot_busy_skip_queue check
- proxy/proxy/session.py: Scheduler parameter in _invalidate_session_and_slot(), SlotLockCoordinator.set_scheduler() method, _scheduler attribute
- proxy/proxy/server.py: _startup_start_scheduler() function and call
- proxy/proxy/ui.py: Scheduler reenter check in model loading endpoint

### Config
- proxy/config.yaml: Remove entire slot_management section

### Tests to update/remove
- proxy/tests/test_slot_scheduler.py (remove)
- proxy/tests/test_slot_scheduler_integration.py (remove)
- proxy/tests/test_cache_rebuild_regression.py (remove -- imports JobScheduler directly)
- proxy/tests/test_disconnect_detection.py (remove JobScheduler sections/tests and patches)
- proxy/tests/test_provider_fallback.py (remove patches and scheduler-related tests)
- proxy/tests/test_local_dispatch_gate.py (remove monkeypatches)
- proxy/tests/test_proxy_to_local_parity.py (remove monkeypatches/mocks)
- proxy/tests/test_local_load_orchestration_parity.py (remove scheduler patches and reenter test)
- proxy/tests/test_resolved_model_header.py (remove monkeypatch)
- proxy/tests/test_abandoned_future.py (remove monkeypatch)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `proxy/proxy/slot_scheduler.py` is deleted entirely
2. All imports and references to `JobScheduler`, `AdmitResult`, `slot_management`, and scheduler-related symbols are removed from:
   - `proxy/proxy/router.py` (globals, getter functions, admission logic, release helper, wiring)
   - `proxy/proxy/provider.py` (scheduler check helpers, slot-busy queue bypass)
   - `proxy/proxy/session.py` (scheduler parameters, `SlotLockCoordinator.set_scheduler`, `_scheduler` attribute)
   - `proxy/proxy/server.py` (`_startup_start_scheduler` function and call)
   - `proxy/proxy/ui.py` (scheduler reenter check in model loading endpoint)
3. The `slot_management` config section is removed from `proxy/config.yaml`, and any cross-references to it are cleaned up
4. All scheduler-related test files are removed or updated so they no longer reference `JobScheduler` or scheduler helpers
5. All remaining tests pass with no regressions after the removal
6. The dispatch lease system (`_try_acquire_local_dispatch`) continues to correctly gate concurrency to `session_slot_pool_size` and release inactive leases after timeout

# Multi-backend: support multiple local llama-server instances with provider-level fallback

## Problem Statement

The proxy currently routes all local-model requests to a single llama-server instance at `http://localhost:8080`, limiting GPU slot capacity to a single server's `-np` value. Users who want to run llama-server on multiple GPUs (same machine or across machines) cannot do so without changes to config, dispatch leases, slot persistence, and health monitoring.

## Users

- **Pi agent operators** who have multiple GPUs (e.g., two $199 GPUs) and want to pool their GPU slot capacity for larger or more concurrent local inference.
- The primary use case is **increasing total GPU slot capacity** by running llama-server on multiple machines (e.g., Server-1 at 192.168.0.199:8080 with `-np 2`, Server-2 at 192.168.0.200:8080 with `-np 1`).

### Example User Stories

> "As an operator with multiple GPU machines, I want to configure two (or more) local llama-server instances in the config so that I can increase my total available GPU slot count."

> "As an operator, I want each local llama-server instance to be self-contained with its own slot cache directory, so that a broken slot on one server doesn't affect the other."

> "As an operator, I want the proxy to fall back through a chain of local servers when one is busy or unhealthy, so that local inference is more available."

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Local llama-server instances can be configured as separate provider entries in `config.yaml`, each with its own `endpoint` URL (host:port) and optionally a `llama_model` field.
2. The dispatch lease system (`_try_acquire_local_dispatch`) is scoped per-endpoint — each server independently tracks its own active session leases, keyed by `(endpoint, session_id)`.
3. Slot save/restore paths are auto-derived per-endpoint under a single global slot cache parent (`session_slot_save_path`), using subdirectories named by the endpoint (host-port).
4. The proxy supports a fallback chain across multiple local providers: when server-1's slots are exhausted or it fails, server-2 (the next `type: local` provider in the chain) is tried automatically.
5. Each local server gets health probes that include: (a) an HTTP health check on its endpoint, (b) GPU OOM detection via error-pattern monitoring, and (c) slot capacity awareness (number of available GPU slots).
6. The proxy assumes pre-existing llama-server instances — no lifecycle management (start/stop/watchdog) for multiple backends is introduced in this work item. However, the architecture must allow lifecycle management to be added later.
7. Full project test suite passes with the new changes.
8. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant config schema docs.

## Constraints

- **Local servers only:** All instances remain `type: local` (not `type: remote`). The local-specific dispatch lease system is maintained but made per-endpoint.
- **Sequential fallback only (no load balancing):** Requests try server-1 first; if exhausted, fall to server-2. Round-robin/load-balancing is out of scope.
- **Pre-existing servers only (no lifecycle management):** The proxy does not start/stop llama-server instances for multiple backends. Single-server startup via `start-llama.sh` continues to work unchanged.
- **Per-server slot save/restore:** Each server gets its own subdirectory under the global `session_slot_save_path`, derived from the endpoint host:port.
- **CHANGELOG.md is excluded** from manual updates — managed by the ship skill's release pipeline.

## Existing State

- `proxy_to_local` in `proxy/proxy/router.py` always targets `http://localhost:{llama_server_port}` (from `server.llama_server_port` in config, default 8080).
- Provider config for `type: local` only supports `llama_model` — no `endpoint` field.
- The dispatch lease system (`_try_acquire_local_dispatch` in `proxy/proxy/router_helpers.py`) uses a global `local_dispatch_records` dict keyed by `session_id` only.
- Slot save/restore uses a single global path (`server.session_slot_save_path`).
- `start-llama.sh` manages a single llama-server process.
- Remote provider fallback already supports ordered fallback across provider entries with per-provider endpoint, concurrency, error handling, and cooldown.

## Desired Change

1. **Provider config support for `type: local`**: Add `endpoint` field support. When specified, the local provider uses that endpoint instead of the global `localhost:{port}`. Backward compatible — omitting `endpoint` falls back to current behavior.

2. **Per-backend dispatch leases**: Change `local_dispatch_records` from a flat dict (keyed by `session_id`) to a two-level structure keyed by `(endpoint_url, session_id)`, so each server tracks its own concurrency independently.

3. **Per-server slot persistence**: Derive each server's slot save subdirectory from its endpoint (e.g., `{session_slot_save_path}/{host}-{port}/`), so slot state from one server doesn't collide with another.

4. **Local fallback chain in provider resolution**: When multiple `type: local` providers are listed for a model, the fallback chain iterates through them. If server-1's dispatch lease acquisition fails (all slots busy), fall through to server-2.

5. **Health probes beyond HTTP**: For `type: local` providers, add GPU OOM error-pattern detection and slot capacity awareness (number of available slots). These supplement the existing HTTP health check.

## Design Sketch

Model each llama-server as a separate entry in the provider chain, similar to how remote providers are listed:

```yaml
models:
  qwen3:
    providers:
      - name: local-qwen3-server-1
        type: local
        llama_model: Qwen3
        endpoint: http://192.168.0.199:8080
      - name: local-qwen3-server-2
        type: local
        llama_model: Qwen3
        endpoint: http://192.168.0.200:8080
      - name: opencode-deepseek-free
        type: remote
        ...
```

Backward compatibility: providers without an `endpoint` field fall back to the existing default (`http://localhost:{server.llama_server_port}`).

## Risks and Assumptions

### Risks

- **Per-endpoint dispatch lease complexity:** If a session holds a dispatch lease on server-1 and server-1 fails, the lease persists until timeout, blocking that session's slot on a healthy server. May need lease-transfer or fast-failure detection.
- **GPU OOM detection fidelity:** llama-server's HTTP API may not expose OOM errors distinctly — the proxy may only see generic 500 responses. Mitigation: monitor error response patterns and slot-capacity changes over time.
- **Advanced scope vs. core scope:** The initial implementation scope (Option C) includes GPU OOM detection and health probes beyond HTTP, which could balloon implementation time. Consider splitting into core (AC 1-4) and advanced health monitoring (AC 5) as separate milestones.
- **Backward compatibility regression:** Existing single-server setups must continue to work unchanged. All config changes for `type: local` must be optional/backward-compatible.

### Assumptions

- Sequential fallback (no load balancing) is sufficient for the primary use case (increasing total GPU slot capacity, not availability).
- Users manage the lifecycle of multiple llama-server instances independently — no proxy-side start/stop/watchdog required.
- The existing remote-provider fallback infrastructure is a suitable model for local-provider fallback (same iteration pattern, error handling, and cooldown).
- Slot save/restore subdirectories derived from endpoint host-port are unique and stable across proxy restarts.

## Related Work

- `LP-0MRHV4UYE0013F6P` — Reduced dispatch lease timeout from 180s to 60s. This work item's per-endpoint leases will use the same timeout logic, per-endpoint.
- `LP-0MR5MAJNM005R905` — Local concurrency limit. The per-endpoint dispatch lease pools will similarly respect `local_max_concurrent_queries` per server.
- `LP-0MRCSSBTM002NK3B` — Large-context cold-cache fallback threshold. When multiple local servers are in the chain, this logic applies per-server based on slot cache state.
- `proxy/proxy/provider.py` lines ~1542-1577 — Remote provider fallback chain is the implementation model for local-provider fallback.
- `proxy/config.yaml` — Current schema and example config for `type: local` and `type: remote` providers.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/provider.py` — Provider resolution and fallback logic. Needs to treat multiple `type: local` entries similarly to multiple remote entries in the chain.
- `proxy/proxy/router.py` — `proxy_to_local` function. Needs to accept dynamic endpoint URLs instead of hardcoded `localhost:{port}`.
- `proxy/proxy/router_helpers.py` — `_try_acquire_local_dispatch`, `_release_local_dispatch`, `_cleanup_stale_dispatch_records`. Needs to key dispatch records per-endpoint.
- `proxy/proxy/server.py` — Config loading/parsing for `type: local` providers. Needs to accept `endpoint` field. Slot save/restore paths are configured via `session_slot_save_path`.
- `proxy/proxy/session.py` — Slot save/restore functions (`_save_slot_snapshot`, `_restore_slot_snapshot`, `_build_slot_context`) use `session_slot_save_path`. Needs per-endpoint subdirectory derivation.
- `proxy/config.yaml` — Schema documentation and example configs updated.
- `start-llama.sh` — No changes expected (lifecycle management out of scope), but may need minor updates for backward compat.

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

- **Q (Round 1, Q1):** "Should local servers be treated identically to remote servers in the provider chain, or kept separate with local-specific dispatch lease, OOM detection, etc.?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option B — Keep local servers separate. Maintain the current local-specific dispatch lease system but key it per-endpoint. Local servers get special handling (GPU OOM detection, slot corruption, lifecycle management) that remote providers don't need.  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 1.

- **Q (Round 1, Q2):** "How should multiple local llama-server instances be managed — pre-existing only, managed by proxy, or both?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option A — Pre-existing only. The proxy connects to llama-server instances that are already running. No start/stop lifecycle management for multiple backends.  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 1.

- **Q (Round 1, Q3):** "Scope for initial implementation: core only, + lifecycle, or + advanced features (per-server slot paths, GPU memory probes, health monitoring)?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option C — Advanced. Core (multiple endpoints in config, per-endpoint dispatch leases, fallback) + per-server slot paths + GPU OOM detection + health monitoring beyond HTTP.  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 1.

- **Q (Round 1, Q4):** "Primary use case priority: increase total GPU slot capacity, improve availability/failover, or both?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option A — Increase total GPU slot capacity (run llama-server on multiple machines).  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 1.

- **Q (Round 2, Q5):** "Where should per-server slot-save paths be stored — configurable per-provider, auto-derived, or single global path with subdirectories?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option C — Single global path (`session_slot_save_path`), each server gets its own subdirectory by endpoint (host-port).  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 2.

- **Q (Round 2, Q6):** "What health checks beyond HTTP should local servers get?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option C — Slot capacity probe + GPU OOM detection (watch for specific error patterns in server logs or responses).  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 2.

- **Q (Round 2, Q7):** "Concurrency model across servers — fallback chain (sequential), round-robin/load-balance, or fallback chain with independent per-server pools?"  
  **A (user@rgardler):** Option A — Fallback chain. Try server-1 first; if exhausted/fail, try server-2 sequentially. Each server has its own independent concurrency pool.  
  **Source:** Interactive reply, Round 2.

The proxy's `/v1/audio/speech` handler forwards the `voice` field directly to the TTS server. The custom_voice model has 9 named speakers (serena, vivian, uncle_fu, ryan, aiden, ono_anna, sohee, eric, dylan) but clients may send OpenAI-style voice names (e.g. `"alloy"`, `"echo"`) which the TTS server rejects.

## Problem statement

When a client sends an unrecognized voice name, the TTS server returns either HTTP 502 ("synthesis failed") or HTTP 200 with 0 bytes of audio — neither useful. The proxy should validate the `voice` field, fall back to `"vivian"` when unrecognized, and signal the fallback via a standard HTTP `Warning` header so clients still get working audio.

## Users

- **Primary**: Developers integrating with the TTS API who may use OpenAI-compatible voice names.
- **Secondary**: End users who should receive working audio regardless of voice name.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The proxy fetches the list of valid TTS voices from the upstream TTS server's `/v1/voices` endpoint and caches it.
2. When an incoming request has a `voice` field that is not in the valid voices list, the proxy substitutes `"vivian"` as the default voice before forwarding to the TTS server.
3. When a voice substitution occurs, the proxy logs a warning and includes a standard HTTP `Warning` header in the response (RFC 7234, code `299`), e.g.: `Warning: 299 proxy "voice='alloy' not recognized, using default 'vivian'"`
4. The audio body is returned unchanged (pure binary PCM/WAV) — no wrapping or restructuring.
5. No voice substitution occurs when the voice IS valid — passes through unchanged.
6. No voice substitution occurs when no `voice` field is provided — matches current handling.
7. Tests verify: (a) valid voice passes through, (b) invalid voice triggers fallback to `vivian` with `Warning` header, (c) no `voice` field works as before, (d) voice list caching works.
8. All related documentation is updated, including code comments and README.
9. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- Must not change the response body format — audio must remain pure binary.
- Must not add new dependencies.
- Must remain backward compatible — existing clients with valid voices see no change.

## Existing state

- The proxy's `create_speech()` handler in `handlers.py` passes `voice` through with no validation.
- The TTS server exposes `/v1/voices` which lists the 9 valid speakers.
- The proxy already has a `/v1/voices` passthrough endpoint (`list_voices()`).

## Desired change

1. In `handlers.py`, fetch and cache the valid voice list from the TTS server.
2. In `create_speech()`, validate `voice` against the cached list before building `forward_body`.
3. On mismatch, substitute `"vivian"`, log the event, and append a `Warning` header to the response.
4. Add tests for the new validation/fallback/warning behavior.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/handlers.py` — Voice validation, fallback, and Warning header logic in `create_speech()`.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_route.py` — Extend with voice validation/fallback test cases.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_integration.py` — Potentially add integration test for fallback behavior.
- `proxy/README.md` — Document the voice fallback behavior.
data.title: Add voice validation with default fallback and Warning header in proxy TTS handler

# Intake Brief: Refactor backend resilience into per-server modules (llama, tts)

## Problem statement

The `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` module (910 lines) contains a mix of shared utility functions, llama-server-specific watchdog/health logic, and TTS-server-specific watchdog/health logic. As the proxy gains support for more backend servers, this monolithic structure will become increasingly tangled. The module needs to be split into per-server modules with a shared utilities core.

## Users

- **Primary**: Developers and maintainers adding or modifying backend-server resilience logic who need clear module boundaries.
- **Secondary**: Code reviewers who benefit from smaller, focused modules.

### User Stories

- As a developer adding support for a new backend server type (e.g., embedding server), I want to add a new self-contained module following the established pattern so that I don't need to untangle the monolithic watchdog code.
- As a maintainer fixing a llama-server watchdog issue, I want to find all llama-specific logic in one module so that I don't risk breaking TTS watchdog behavior.
- As a developer debugging TTS self-healing, I want TTS-specific functions isolated in their own module so that I can understand them independently.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Each backend server type (llama, TTS) has its own module under `proxy/proxy/backends/` with its watchdog, health probing, and recovery logic.
2. `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` retains only shared utilities (backoff helpers, pruning, signal recording, coerce functions, `_self_healing_response()`, `_worker_process_unhealthy()`, `_extract_model_port_from_args()`, `_srv()`).
3. `proxy/proxy/backends/__init__.py` and module files (`llama.py`, `tts.py`) are created with clean module-level exports.
4. Backward-compatible re-exports are added to `backend_health.py` so that existing imports from `proxy.backend_health` continue to work without modification.
5. All existing tests (`test_backend_resilience.py`, `test_tts_health_endpoint.py`, `test_tts_watchdog.py`) pass without modification.
6. The `lifecycle.py` re-exports and `router_helpers.py` imports continue to work without changes.
7. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.
8. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.

> **Note:** CHANGELOG.md is **excluded** from this list. It is managed automatically by the ship skill's release pipeline.

## Constraints

- **No functional changes**: Pure refactoring — no behavior changes, no new features, no bug fixes.
- **Backward-compatible imports**: All existing import paths (`from proxy.backend_health import ...`) must continue to work via re-exports.
- **No new dependencies**: Use only existing imports (asyncio, subprocess, httpx, fastapi).
- **Module naming**: Follow existing Python package conventions — `proxy/proxy/backends/` as a package with `llama.py` and `tts.py` modules.

## Existing state

- `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` (910 lines) contains all functions inline:
  - **Shared utilities** (~10 functions): `_srv()`, `_self_heal_retry_after_seconds()`, `_is_self_healing_active()`, `_self_healing_response()`, `_backend_recovery_snapshot()`, `_worker_process_unhealthy()`, `_prune_recovery_attempts()`, `_coerce_float()`, `_coerce_int()`, `_extract_model_port_from_args()`
  - **Llama-specific** (~5 functions): `_attempt_router_self_heal()`, `_backend_watchdog_loop()`, `_router_model_health_loop()`, `_probe_model_instance_with_retries()`, `_probe_model_instance()`
  - **TTS-specific** (~7 functions): `_get_tts_watchdog_interval()`, `_get_tts_self_heal_max_attempts()`, `_get_tts_self_heal_window()`, `_get_tts_self_heal_probe_timeout()`, `_tts_recovery_snapshot()`, `_attempt_tts_self_heal()`, `_tts_watchdog_loop()`
- `proxy/proxy/lifecycle.py` re-exports functions from `backend_health.py` with `# noqa: F401` comments.
- `proxy/proxy/router_helpers.py` imports `_self_heal_retry_after_seconds` directly from `proxy.backend_health`.
- Test files (`test_backend_resilience.py`, `test_tts_watchdog.py`) import from `proxy.backend_health`.
- No `proxy/proxy/backends/` package directory exists yet.

## Desired change

1. Create `proxy/proxy/backends/` package directory with `__init__.py`.
2. Create `proxy/proxy/backends/llama.py` with all llama-specific watchdog/health functions.
3. Create `proxy/proxy/backends/tts.py` with all TTS-specific watchdog/health functions.
4. Strip `backend_health.py` to only shared utilities.
5. Add re-exports in `backend_health.py` for backward compatibility (`from .backends.llama import ...`, `from .backends.tts import ...`).
6. Update `lifecycle.py` re-exports to import from the new modules instead (or continue via `backend_health.py` re-exports).
7. Verify all existing imports and tests continue to work.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` — Strip to shared utilities only; add backward-compatible re-exports.
- `proxy/proxy/backends/__init__.py` — New file; package init for the backends subpackage.
- `proxy/proxy/backends/llama.py` — New file; llama-specific watchdog/health functions extracted from `backend_health.py`.
- `proxy/proxy/backends/tts.py` — New file; TTS-specific watchdog/health functions extracted from `backend_health.py`.
- `proxy/proxy/lifecycle.py` — Update re-imports if they change (may continue via re-exports in `backend_health.py`).

## Related work

- **Extend self-healing to monitor and revive TTS server (LP-0MRPHQZ2M003X5YU)** — Completed. Added TTS watchdog functions to `backend_health.py`. This refactor was discovered-from that work item to avoid further tangling.
- **Extract backend recovery and health monitoring to backend_health.py (LP-0MQCT86UZ00387D0)** — Completed. The original extraction from `lifecycle.py` to `backend_health.py`. This work follows the same pattern for further decomposition.
- **Add TTS watchdog loop for automatic restart (LP-0MRT928DD008136S)** — Completed child of LP-0MRPHQZ2M003X5YU. Established the TTS watchdog functions that will be moved to `backends/tts.py`.
- **Detect and self-heal llama-server GPU crash states via health endpoint (LP-0MQ0ZHA4H006TUNE)** — Completed. Established the original watchdog pattern that this refactor builds on.

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Risk**: Missed import paths causing runtime breakage. **Mitigation**: Full test suite must pass; grep all `from proxy.backend_health import` to ensure no missed paths.
- **Risk**: Circular imports if backends modules import from each other. **Mitigation**: Each backend module must only import from `backend_health.py` (shared utilities), not from sibling modules.
- **Risk**: Tests monkey-patch `backend_health` module attributes (e.g., `_probe_model_instance_with_retries`). After extraction, patches must reference the correct module. **Mitigation**: Backward-compatible re-exports preserve the `backend_health` namespace so existing monkey patches continue to work. Verify with test suite.
- **Risk**: The `server.py` lifespan creates watchdog tasks via functions accessed as `srv.<function>()` through the lazy server import. If the import chain (`lifecycle.py` → `backend_health.py` → `backends/llama.py`) breaks, runtime crashes on startup. **Mitigation**: Re-exports in `backend_health.py` preserve the full import chain. Verify with test suite.
- **Scope-creep risk**: Temptation to refactor or rename functions during extraction. **Mitigation**: Strictly move code without renaming or changing signatures.
- **Assumption**: No external code outside `proxy/` imports from `backend_health.py`.
- **Assumption**: The `_srv()` lazy import mechanism works identically from any subpackage module (circular import safety depends on `proxy.server` import at call time, not import time).

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: "Should the refactored modules use the same private (`_`-prefixed) function names or should some be made public?" — Answer: Keep same private names. This is a pure relocation refactor — no API changes. Source: work item description already states "No functional changes — pure refactoring with no behavior changes."
- Q: "What about `_extract_model_port_from_args()` — is it llama-specific or shared?" — Answer: It is used by `_router_model_health_loop()` (llama-specific). However, since it is a pure utility (no server state dependency), it can remain as a shared utility in `backend_health.py` for reuse. Source: code review — function is a pure parsing utility.
- Q: "Should `_worker_process_unhealthy()` be shared or per-server?" — Answer: It is a general process-health check utility used by the llama watchdog. It's server-agnostic (takes `proc: subprocess.Popen | None`) and should remain shared. Source: code review — function signature and logic have no server-specific dependencies.
data.title: Refactor backend resilience into per-server modules (llama, tts)

## Summary

Add `tts_server_running`, `tts_server_healthy`, and `tts_enabled` fields to the `/health` endpoint so operators can see TTS server status at a glance.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `/health` response includes `tts_server_running: bool` — reflects whether `tts_process.poll() is None` (process alive).
2. `/health` response includes `tts_server_healthy: bool` — determined by probing `http://localhost:<tts_port>/health` (which returns `{"status": "ok"}`).
3. `/health` response includes `tts_enabled: bool` from config so operators can distinguish disabled from crashed.
4. A helper function `_probe_tts_health()` (or similar) performs the HTTP health probe with a short timeout (default 2s).
5. Tests verify all three states: (a) TTS alive — process running and health probe succeeds, (b) TTS dead — process exited or health probe fails, (c) TTS disabled — `tts_enabled=false` returns running=false and healthy=false.
6. Full test suite passes.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/handlers.py` — Extend `health_check()` with TTS fields and probe helper.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_integration.py` — Add health endpoint tests.

## Dependencies

- None

## Summary

Add a background `_tts_watchdog_loop()` that monitors the TTS process and automatically restarts it when it exits or becomes unhealthy, respecting `tts_enabled`.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `_tts_watchdog_loop()` in `backend_health.py` periodically checks `tts_process.poll()` at a configurable interval (default 10s).
2. When the process has exited, the watchdog restarts it via `start_tts_server()` with retry backoff and configurable max attempts within a time window.
3. Config keys added to `config.yaml`:
   - `tts_self_heal_max_attempts` (default: 3)
   - `tts_self_heal_window_seconds` (default: 120)
   - `tts_self_heal_interval_seconds` (default: 10)
   - `tts_self_heal_probe_timeout_seconds` (default: 3)
4. Watchdog respects `tts_enabled=false` — no monitoring or restart when disabled.
5. Watchdog is wired into `server.py` lifespan: started alongside existing `_backend_watchdog_loop` and cancelled on shutdown.
6. Failed restart attempts are logged clearly (same detail level as llama-server recovery).
7. Tests verify: (a) watchdog restarts a dead TTS process within configured limits, (b) watchdog does not monitor when `tts_enabled=false`, (c) health endpoint reflects recovery states during restart attempts.
8. Full test suite passes.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/backend_health.py` — Add `_tts_watchdog_loop()` and helper functions.
- `proxy/proxy/server.py` — Wire TTS watchdog launch/shutdown into lifespan.
- `proxy/config.yaml` — Add TTS self-heal configuration defaults.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_watchdog.py` — New file for TTS watchdog self-healing tests.

## Dependencies

- Blocked by: Feature 1 (health endpoint TTS status) — watchdog recovery states should be reflected in `/health` fields.

# New home page showing model endpoints with activity state

## Problem Statement

The proxy server's web interface currently shows a page with a model table, API endpoint docs, and admin controls. However, there is no dedicated view that surfaces per-model endpoint configuration details (including fallback providers) alongside real-time activity state such as active/in-flight query counts. Operators need a single view to see which models are configured, their provider endpoints, and how much load each is currently handling.

## Users

- **Operators/SREs** monitoring model health, traffic distribution, and endpoint configurations.
- **Developers** who need to verify model routing, provider fallbacks, and active request counts during testing.
- **On-call engineers** who need to quickly identify which models are under load or misconfigured.

### User stories

- As an operator, I want to see all configured models and their provider endpoints (including fallback providers) in one place so I can verify the routing setup at a glance.
- As an on-call engineer, I want to see how many active queries each model is handling so I can quickly identify traffic spikes or backpressure issues.
- As a developer, I want the new home page to be the default tab so I always land on the endpoint/activity view when opening the proxy UI.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A new tab/section visible on the proxy web interface shows a table or list of all configured models with:
   - Model name/ID
   - Type (local/remote)
   - Primary endpoint URL (local llama-server address or remote API endpoint)
   - Fallback provider entries (if configured), each with endpoint and type
2. For each model, the interface displays the current number of **active queries/in-flight requests**.
   - Per-model active query counters are derived from existing tracking mechanisms or new per-model counters.
   - Models with no active requests display `0`.
   - Models where tracking is unavailable (e.g., remote-only with no new counter yet) display `-` or `0`.
3. The new tab is the **default view** — when navigating to the proxy web interface root (`/`), users see this tab first.
4. An SSE-based or polled mechanism keeps the activity counters updated in real time without requiring a full page refresh. The existing `/events` SSE endpoint is extended to include per-model active query data (e.g., a `per_model_queries` key).
5. The existing index page content (model table, quick test, API endpoint docs) remains accessible via a tab bar or navigation links within the page.
6. Activity counters gracefully handle unknown/unavailable values (e.g., display `0` or `-` when no data).
7. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
8. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.

## Constraints

- **Data source:** Active query counters are maintained in `proxy/server.py` (`active_queries` global, `local_active_queries`, `local_dispatch_records`). However, these are global/session-level counters — **there is no existing per-model breakdown**. The implementing agent will need to add per-model tracking. See Risks & Assumptions below.
- **Model config:** Per-model endpoint and provider (including fallback) data comes from `srv.config["models"]` dict and the `providers` list within each model config. Use existing helpers in `proxy/provider.py` to extract details.
- **UI pattern:** Must fit alongside the existing `index.html` template. Use the same CSS variables and design system to maintain visual consistency.
- **No new dependencies:** The SSE mechanism already exists (`/events` endpoint in `proxy/ui.py`). Extend it rather than adding a new streaming mechanism.

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Assumption: Per-model active query tracking can be added without significant rework.** The existing `local_dispatch_records` stores `backend` (not `model`) per session. To derive per-model counts, the implementation should either (a) add a `model` field to dispatch records, (b) create per-model counters alongside the existing global ones, or (c) infer the model from the session key. The simplest approach is likely adding per-model counters to `_increment_local_active_queries` / `_decrement_local_active_queries` and `_increment_active_queries` / `_decrement_active_queries`.
- **Risk: Remote model tracking is purely global.** `active_queries` is a single integer — no per-remote-model tracking exists. For models routed through remote providers, per-model active counts may initially show aggregate or need a new counter per remote model.
- **Risk: Scope creep.** This feature could expand into a full monitoring dashboard (charts, historical data, provider health). The scope is limited to: (a) display per-model endpoint configuration, (b) show current active query count per model, (c) tab-based UI alongside existing content.
- **Assumption: SSE payload extension is backward compatible.** Adding `per_model_queries` to the existing `/events` SSE payload is a pure extension — existing clients ignore unknown fields.

## Existing State

- The proxy web interface serves a single `index.html` template rendered by the `index()` handler in `proxy/ui.py`.
- The template includes a status bar, model table, quick test panel, API endpoint documentation, and admin actions.
- Real-time updates are delivered via SSE at `/events` (`status_events()` in `proxy/ui.py`), which currently broadcasts: `current_model`, `loaded_models`, `llama_server_running`, `n_ctx`, `kv_cache_tokens`, `total_sent`, `total_recv`.
- Active query tracking: `proxy/server.py` maintains `active_queries` (int), `active_queries_lock`, `local_active_queries` (int), `local_active_queries_lock`, `local_dispatch_records` (dict with per-session active/inactive + expires_at tracking).
- Model configuration is stored in `srv.config["models"]` (loaded from models.ini, etc.). Each model can have multiple providers in a `providers` list for fallback routing.
- SSE client tracking is done via `srv.sse_clients` (set of Queue objects).

## Desired Changes

### Server-side (`proxy/server.py`)
- Expose per-model active query counts in the SSE broadcasts. This may require maintaining a per-model counter or deriving it from existing data structures.

### Server-side (`proxy/ui.py`)
- Extend the `status_events()` SSE endpoint to include per-model activity data (e.g., a `per_model_queries` dictionary mapping model_name → active count).
- Add a new route to serve the home page content (or add it as a template section). Alternatively, modify the `index()` handler to inject a table of model endpoints with activity data.

### Client-side (`proxy/templates/index.html`)
- Add a **tab bar** at the top of the page with tabs: "Home" (new, default), "Models" (existing model table), and "API" (existing API endpoint docs).
- The "Home" tab displays a table/list of all models with: name, type, endpoint, fallback providers, and active queries count.
- Wire the SSE handler to update the per-model active query counters in real time.
- Ensure the tab state persists across page navigation (sessionStorage or URL hash).

### Tests
- Playwright tests for the new tab: asserting the model list renders, activity counters appear and update.
- Unit tests for any new server-side data extraction/computation helpers.

## Key Files

- `proxy/server.py` — Server state including `active_queries`, `local_active_queries`, `local_dispatch_records`, SSE broadcast logic. Likely needs to expose per-model active counts.
- `proxy/ui.py` — Web UI handlers (`index()`, `status_events()`, `view_logs()`). Needs the SSE payload extended and potentially a new template section.
- `proxy/templates/index.html` — The single-page template. Needs tab bar and Home tab content added.
- `proxy/provider.py` — Helpers `get_model_type()`, `get_local_model_name_from_providers()`, `get_remote_endpoint()` used to extract per-model endpoint info.
- `proxy/router_helpers.py` — Active query increment/decrement helpers to understand how to derive per-model counts.

## Related Work

- **LP-0MN5AW8DE1KJVAKX** — Add stats to the main page for the currently loaded model (completed). Added stats panel, `query_llama_status()` helper, and expanded SSE payload with `n_ctx`/`kv_cache_tokens`. The new home page can reuse the same SSE extension pattern.
- **LP-0MQ0PYH8P008DLPJ** — Web based logging per provider/model/session (completed). Related tabbed UI and SSE streaming for logs.
- **LP-0MRIL2L3E0080OGC** — Harden `_decrement_local_active_queries` against silent counter leaks (completed). Relevant for accurate active query counting.

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

- Q: "What counts as an 'endpoint'? Options: A) All known API endpoint paths (e.g., /v1/chat/completions), B) Per-model configuration entries with provider/endpoint details, C) Both." — Answer (user): "B". Source: interactive reply.
- Q: "What is 'activity state'? Options: A) Is the model loaded/accepting requests, B) Active queries/in-flight requests per model, C) Provider health, D) Combination." — Answer (user): "B". Source: interactive reply.
- Q: "Relationship to existing homepage: A) Replace the index, B) Add as new tab alongside existing content, C) Replace just the model table portion." — Answer (user): "B — and the new tab is the default". Source: interactive reply.

# LLama Proxy Server drops lang field from TTS requests to qwentts.cpp

## Problem Statement

The LLama Proxy Server's `/v1/audio/speech` handler silently drops the `lang` field from incoming TTS requests before forwarding them to the qwentts.cpp backend. This means per-request language preferences (e.g., `lang: "english"`) never reach the TTS model, causing the backend to use its startup default (`--lang english` or `auto`), which can result in mixed-language audio output (e.g., English/Chinese).

## Users

- **End users** who make TTS requests that include a `lang` field and expect English-only audio output.
- **API consumers (tts_generate.py)** which sends `lang: "english"` in every TTS request and gets mixed-language output.
- **Operators** who deploy the proxy with the TTS pipeline and receive complaints about poor audio quality.

### User Stories

- As an API consumer, I want the `lang` field I send in my TTS request to be passed through to the TTS backend so the output language matches my request.
- As an operator, I want the proxy to faithfully forward all TTS parameters to the backend so that language handling is consistent.
- As a developer, I want the proxy's TTS handler to be fully transparent with respect to the backend API capabilities.

## Evidence

1. **Live TTS server process confirmed running with `--lang english`**:
   ```
   ./tts-server ... --port 8081 --lang english
   ```
   Option B is already deployed but insufficient.

2. **Per-request `lang` field is supported by the tts-server API**:
   - `curl` POST with `"lang": "english"` returns 200 with different output characteristics (165 KB vs 96 KB without lang).
   - The binary has internal language model data (`qwen3-tts.codec.language_ids`, `qwen3-tts.codec.language_names`) and validation logic (`[Prompt] FATAL: unknown language '%s'`).

3. **Proxy handler silently drops `lang`**:
   - `handlers.py:create_speech()` (line 813) reads `model`, `input`, `voice`, `response_format`, `instructions` but NOT `lang`.
   - The `forward_body` dict constructed at line 878 never includes `lang`.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The proxy's `POST /v1/audio/speech` handler reads the optional `lang` field from the incoming request body and forwards it to the tts-server backend when present.
2. When `lang` is absent from the request, the handler must not add it to the forwarded body (backward compatible).
3. The `lang` field is documented in the proxy's API contract (OpenAPI spec and/or docstring) as an optional parameter.
4. All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
5. Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.
6. Tests are written to verify:
   - `lang` field is forwarded to tts-server when provided in the request.
   - `lang` is NOT forwarded when absent (backward compatibility).
   - Invalid `lang` values are still passed through (backend validation, not proxy concern).

> **Note:** CHANGELOG.md is excluded from this list. It is managed automatically by the ship skill's release pipeline.

## Constraints

- No new dependencies or libraries.
- The `lang` field must be optional and backward-compatible.
- The proxy must not validate the `lang` value — that is the backend's responsibility.
- The fix should be minimal: add `lang` to the fields read from the request body and include it in `forward_body` when present.

## Existing State

- **TTS server startup:** `proxy/proxy/lifecycle.py:start_tts_server()` passes `--lang english` at line 1130. The running server confirms this flag is active.
- **Proxy handler:** `proxy/proxy/handlers.py:create_speech()` reads `model`, `input`, `voice`, `response_format`, `instructions` from the request body but NOT `lang`. The `forward_body` dict at line 878 omits `lang`.
- **Backend API:** The qwentts.cpp tts-server (`bb250f5`) supports `lang` as both a CLI startup flag (`--lang <name>`, default: `auto`) and a per-request JSON field in the POST body. The model GGUF contains language metadata (`qwen3-tts.codec.language_ids`, `qwen3-tts.codec.language_names`).
- **Tests:** The existing contract tests in `proxy/tests/test_tts_route.py` (`test_request_passthrough_forwards_all_params`) verify `model`, `input`, `voice`, `response_format`, `instructions` are forwarded — but NOT `lang`.
- **Documentation:** The proxy README's `/v1/audio/speech` section lists `model`, `input`, `voice`, `response_format` but not `lang`.

## Desired Change

1. In `proxy/proxy/handlers.py:create_speech()`, add:
   ```python
   lang = body.get("lang", "")
   ```
   alongside the existing optional parameter reads (line ~847).
2. Add to `forward_body` when present:
   ```python
   if lang:
       forward_body["lang"] = lang
   ```
3. Update the docstring and README to document `lang` as an optional field.
4. Update the contract test to verify `lang` is forwarded when provided, and absent when not provided.

## Key Files

- `proxy/proxy/handlers.py` — The `create_speech()` handler that currently drops `lang`. Add `lang` passthrough.
- `proxy/tests/test_tts_route.py` — Contract tests for the TTS route. Add `lang` forwarding tests.
- `proxy/README.md` — API documentation for `/v1/audio/speech`. Add `lang` to the request fields table.
- `proxy/proxy/lifecycle.py` — Already passes `--lang english` at startup (no change needed, but note for context).

## Related Work

- **LP-0MQVJ7CXE002U3Z0** — Proxy /v1/audio/speech Route (completed): Originally implemented the TTS proxy route.
- **LP-0MQVJ4BP2002O0CX** — TTS API Contract Tests & Mock Route Tests (completed): Established the existing contract tests.
- **LP-0MRO4L9930057AL3** — Add instructions passthrough support to proxy TTS handler (completed): Similar pattern of adding an optional field passthrough (`instructions`). 
- **LP-0MQVJ9TRP002UU0S** — TTS Documentation (completed): Documentation for the TTS pipeline.
- **LP-0MRJ5GO7I005NQI7** — Accumulated config, documentation, and TTS improvements (completed): Added `--lang english` startup flag in commit 9426afc (Option B).

## Risks & Assumptions

- **Per-request lang may not fully resolve mixed-language output.** The Qwen3-TTS model itself is multilingual and may produce mixed-language output regardless of the `lang` field. This fix ensures the proxy faithfully forwards the client's stated language preference, but if the model does not strictly honor per-request `lang`, the output quality may not improve. This risk is out of scope for the proxy and belongs to the model/tts-server upstream.
- **Scope creep risk:** This work item is narrowly scoped to adding `lang` field passthrough. Opportunities to add other missing fields (e.g., `speed`, custom model parameters) or to implement server-side language validation should be tracked as separate work items.
- **Assumption: Backward compatibility is maintained.** Adding `lang` as an optional field must not break existing clients that do not send `lang`.
- **Assumption: The tts-server internally validates the `lang` value.** The proxy should pass through any `lang` value without validation.

## Appendix: Clarifying Questions & Answers

- Q: "Is the mixed-language TTS issue still occurring in your environment?" — Answer (user): "yes, investigate". Source: interactive reply.
- Q: "Does the qwentts.cpp server API support a `lang` field in the per-request body?" — Answer (investigation): "Yes. Confirmed via curl POST with `lang: 'english'` → 200. The binary has language metadata (language_ids, language_names) and validation logic. The output file size differs between requests with and without `lang` (165 KB vs 96 KB), confirming the field is processed by the model." Source: binary strings analysis + curl test.
- Q: "Is Option B (`--lang english` startup) already deployed?" — Answer (investigation): "Yes. Confirmed via `ps aux`: `tts-server ... --model ... --codec ... --port 8081 --lang english`. Also in lifecycle.py line 1130, committed as part of LP-0MRJ5GO7I005NQI7 (commit 9426afc, present on dev and main)." Source: process inspection + git history.
- Q: "Should we implement Option A (per-request lang passthrough) since Option B alone isn't sufficient?" — Answer (user): "proceed". Source: interactive reply.
data.title: LLama Proxy Server drops lang field from TTS requests to qwentts.cpp
